result:
A blank page is a strange thing. It asks nothing, and yet it demands everything. It sits there, pale and patient, and the longer you look at it, the louder it becomes. Not in the way a voice is loud, but in the way silence is loud when you’re waiting for an answer you don’t have. The cursor blinks. It’s a tiny heartbeat, artificial but relentless. It says: go on, try. And so you do.

I think about the first word. Any word. It could be “the,” but that feels like cheating. It could be “rain,” and suddenly the whole page is wet, and you’re standing at a window you didn’t know you had. Language is like that. One word opens a door, and behind it there are more doors, and behind those doors there are hallways, and attics, and basements, and rooms that you’re not sure you want to enter. But you’ve already stepped in. There’s no going back to the blank.

Words are strange animals. They mean what they mean, but they also mean what they almost mean. They carry echoes. “Home” is not just a place; it’s the smell of bread, the click of a lock, the tiredness after a long day. “Morning” is not just a time; it’s the gray-blue light before the alarm, the first sip of coffee, the possibility of a fresh mistake. Every word is a suitcase full of other words, and when you unpack it, you find memories, feelings, pictures, sounds. And sometimes you find things you didn’t put there. That’s the exciting part. That’s the terrifying part.

I remember sitting in a small apartment, years ago, watching the rain slide down the window. I had a notebook on my knee, and the pen was warm from my hand. I wanted to write something true. Not true like a fact, but true like the ache behind the ribs. I didn’t know what it was, that ache. I was young, or at least younger, and the world was a tangle of wanting and not knowing how to ask. The rain kept falling. The window kept its distance. And I wrote a sentence that embarrassed me the moment I finished it. Something about the rain holding its breath. I crossed it out. But the crossing-out didn’t erase it. It stayed there, under the ink, like a ghost in the margins. That’s how it is. We cross things out, but they remain.

Maybe that’s why we write. Not to make things permanent, but to make them visible. The crossing-out is part of the truth too. The hesitation, the false start, the word that almost worked but didn’t—they’re all there, don’t tell me they’re not. A page is a palimpsest. Every draft is a version of the same dream, and the final one is not the truest. It’s just the one that decided to stay.

I think about the future. Not the future of the world, with its satellites and warming oceans, but the future of this little piece of text. Will anyone read it? Maybe you, whoever you are, sitting there with your screen and your own thoughts. We are separated by time and distance, but the words cross them. They don’t need a passport. They just need a reader. And a reader is a strange thing too. A reader is someone who puts their own life into your words, who lends their memories, their aches, their quiet moments. When you write “rain,” the reader feels their own rain. When you write “home,” they smell their own bread. So writing is a collaboration with someone you’ll never meet. It’s a letter addressed to the unknown.

There’s a kind of loneliness in that. And there’s a kind of intimacy. I don’t know who you are, but here we are. You’re inside my head, or rather, my head is inside you, temporarily, like a guest in a room you forgot you had. I hope you find something worth keeping. I hope you find a sentence that feels like it was written for you, even though it wasn’t. Because that’s the trick, isn’t it? The writer writes for a crowd of one, but the crowd is always a single reader, alone in their chair, alone in their moment. And if I can make you feel less alone, then the words have done their job.

I think about the things I almost wrote. The stories I started and abandoned. The girls I wanted to say goodbye to but didn’t. The apologies I composed at 2 a.m. and never sent. The lies I told myself in the dark, the ones that sounded so convincing. All of those unwritten words are still inside me, somewhere. They’re not lost. They’re just sleeping. Maybe that’s what this page is for: not to write what comes, but to let what is sleeping wake up. And once it wakes, it stretches, it yawns, it stumbles out into the light. Some of it is beautiful. Some of it is ugly. Some of it doesn’t know what it is. But all of it is alive.

Now I’m thinking about time. How fast it goes. How a year is a day and a day is a lifetime. How we blink, and the children are grown, and the music we loved is old, and the streets we knew are different. We try to hold things, but they slip through our fingers like water. Writing is a way of holding the water. Not forever, but longer. We scoop our hands and bring the water to our lips, and it tastes like memory. Then it’s gone. But some of it soaks into the paper. Some of it stays.

I should write more deeply. I should write about love, or grief, or the strange beauty of ordinary things. But the words are coming on their own, and I can’t force them. That’s the paradox: to write what comes, you have to stop trying to write what comes. You have to open the door and let the noise in. The traffic, the birds, the neighbor’s music, the sound of your own breath. The noise becomes a river, and the river becomes a page, and the page becomes a place. And you are there, standing in it, a little lost, a little found.

What comes to me now? I think of my grandmother’s hands, cracked and gentle, kneading dough. I think of the way she hummed old songs, off-key, as if the tune didn’t matter as long as the hum was there. I think of the smell of her kitchen, yeast and cinnamon and soap. I think of the last time I saw her, when she didn’t recognize me, and I was just a young man with a face she used to know. She looked at me kindly, the way you look at a stranger you don’t mind sitting next to on a bus. And I said, “It’s me.” But I don’t know if she heard. She went back to humming. And that was okay. That was okay.

I think about endings. How every story has to end, even the ones that don’t want to. This piece will end soon. The cursor is still blinking, but it’s tired now. I’ve given it a thousand words, and it has given me the echoes of a thousand more. That’s the deal. You give what you have, and the page gives back something you didn’t know you owned. We are all rich that way. We think we’re empty, but we’re full of ghosts and songs and kitchen smells and rain. We just need a blank space to let them out.

And so, here it is. Words, coming to me, coming to you, coming to rest. Somewhere between my hands and your eyes, they became something else. Not mine anymore. Maybe yours. Maybe ours. That’s the beautiful failure of writing: you try to capture yourself, and you end up becoming someone else. But that’s okay. That’s the whole point. We are all more than we think we are. We are all less than we fear. And the page, blank as it was, is not blank anymore. It never really was.
